# Appendix B: Software and reproducibility {#sec-appx-software .appendix}

The software stack is the same as papers 1, 2a, 2b and 3's, described in
full in paper 1's Appendix B: R, the tidyverse, `{DBI}`/`{RMariaDB}` for
the Smartform database, `{renv}` for package pinning, `{targets}` for the
pipeline, and Quarto for typesetting. `{mlogit}` fits the blend directly,
as it fits the conditional logits of papers 1 to 2b — `{tidymodels}` has
no conditional-logit engine, and the same documented exception applies.

Three things are specific to this paper.

**A separate pipeline and a separate store.** Paper 4 runs from its own
script, `_targets_p4.R`, into its own store, `_targets_p4`, rather than
sharing the pipeline papers 1 to 3 use. Papers 2b and 3 are inputs here,
and reading them from a pipeline that could also rebuild them invites a
class of accident this paper cannot afford: nothing paper 4 does is
allowed to alter a published result. The upstream targets are read from
the main store read-only, and their content hashes are recorded in a
`p4_upstream_fingerprint` target, so that if a paper 2b or 3 result ever
changes, every paper-4 target downstream of it is invalidated rather than
silently going stale.

The two are run separately:

``` r
targets::tar_make()                                        # papers 1-3
targets::tar_make(script = "_targets_p4.R",                # paper 4
                  store  = "_targets_p4")
```

Unlike papers 1 to 3, this document does not call
`targets::tar_config_set()` in its setup chunk. That function writes the
project-root `_targets.yaml`, which papers 1 to 3's setup chunks also
write; pointing it at the paper-4 store would send their next render at
the wrong store. Paper 4 passes `store =` to each `tar_load()` call
instead and leaves `_targets.yaml` alone.

**Verification gates.** Two standing checks guard this paper, in addition
to the series' existing ones. `scripts/verify_p4_market_probs.R` asserts
that paper 4's market-probability helper is the same arithmetic paper 1
§5.1 already applies to starting prices, by rebuilding the stored
`win_market` column of paper 3's test predictions from raw prices and
requiring agreement to $10^{-12}$; observed agreement is exact. It also
checks that probabilities sum to one within race, that the construction
is invariant to a uniform rescaling of prices, that the freshly pulled
starting prices match the stored ones, and that the price join cannot fan
out. `scripts/verify_p4_data_targets.R` ties @sec-data's live targets to
the standalone P4-0 audit that gated the paper, and asserts that the
distributional summaries touch no test race.

**What was fitted, and what was not.** Papers 2b and 3 are not refitted
anywhere in this paper; their stored test-set predictions are read as
given. The only models fitted here are the blends themselves and their
market-only references, each a one- or two-parameter conditional logit.
The complete pipeline, including the database pulls, runs in well under a
minute — which is the point made in @sec-conclusion about the cost of
this paper relative to the work it informs.

One departure from the series template is worth recording so it reads as
deliberate. Papers 1 to 3 answer three questions — ranking, win-picking
and betting value. This paper answers the first kind of question only and
has no betting-value section, for the reason given in @sec-intro: a blend
that tracks the starting price bets into the starting price's own margin,
so its backtest has a foregone conclusion.
